content: About 22 miles south of the former mining town of Patagonia, Arizona, down a winding, unpaved mountain road that passes cows grazing on open range, stands a cottonwood tree believed to be at least 200 years old. The “grandmother” tree, as some locals call it, is imperiled and already showing signs of stress, almost as if it knows its fate. The leaves are yellowing prematurely, falling to the ground at the height of summer. On July 27th, a construction crew felled three neighboring trees to build an extension of President Donald Trump’s wall along the US-Mexico border. An activist climbed up the last tree standing two days later and ever since, someone has sat on a platform hoisted onto the tree’s branches. They say they’ll sit there as long as it takes, because as long as someone is in the tree, it can’t be cut down. The protest is about more than one cottonwood. “This tree represents a literal line in the sand against border militarization in general,” said Russ McSpadden, the Southwest conservation advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity. In recent weeks, the Department of Homeland Security has revived its effort to wall off the border, dispatching construction crews to remote parts of Texas, Arizona, and the Tohono O’odham Nation’s reservation lands to finish Trump’s wall — and has waived environmental laws to get it built, causing backlash from the tiny desert town of Ajo to the even tinier ghost town of Terlingua. This latest construction push is happening despite record-low encounters along the southwestern border. In fact, encounters at the southwest border dropped almost immediately after Trump took office — not because of any new infrastructure, but because he effectively shut down asylum. Despite the steep decline in migrant crossings, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed along party lines in 2025, gave Trump an additional $46.5 billion to finish building the wall.  The border wall is more than just a wall; it’s a vast surveillance network of interconnected drones, towers, and cameras. Even in areas where there’s no visible barrier separating the United States and Mexico, CBP relies on this “virtual wall” to track migrants. This vast surveillance apparatus is far more effective than a wall, and it’s already largely in place. In the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona, activists from surrounding communities have set up an encampment on private property near the cottonwood tree to support the protest. They take turns cooking meals and use a pulley system to transport food and water to the person sitting in the tree. They know they’re being watched. Trucks from Vision Quest Solutions, a private security firm that advertises itself as veteran- and Native American-owned, roll up and down the fresh dirt road just south of the tree. The activists track the various contractors that are building the road: Fisher Sand & Gravel, BJ Drilling, Stinger Bridge & Iron, and others. [Image: Homeland Security contractors drive past an ancient cottonwood tree in Lochiel, Arizona. Activists have been occupying the tree since July 29th. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/border_wall_tree_sit_e6f222.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Henry, a community organizer from Tucson who is participating in the encampment, said that a DHS helicopter flew “dangerously close” to the tree on August 10th.  “This movement was started and held down for a long time by local environmentalists who care really deeply about these ancient cottonwood trees,” said Henry, who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym. He is among a newer group of activists “who see it as an opportunity to physically stop border wall construction.” The planned construction projects differ by region. In Arizona’s San Rafael Valley, where an older fence already divides Mexico and the United States, DHS is building a wall featuring 30-foot-tall steel bollards. The plan is to have a “double wall” throughout the Arizona-Mexico border — one that runs through the Tohono O’odham reservation, Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, and the San Rafael Valley. To achieve this, DHS contractors are tearing down the old fence, replacing it with the new bollards, and building an entirely new wall a few dozen feet away. The cottonwood tree sits directly in the path of the second wall. “They’re approaching the tree from both sides with their work crews,” Henry said. “I don’t really know what their plan is once they don’t have anything else to do.” In Big Bend National Park, Customs and Border Protection is building what it calls a “Technology & Patrol Road,” or a “smart wall” system of sensors, cameras, and surveillance towers accessible via a new road — even though there’s an existing road that cuts through the park. Responding to mass outcry about recent construction in Big Bend, CBP chief Rodney Scott said that DHS isn’t building a wall. “CBP is building one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations,” Scott said in an emailed statement. “What people are seeing right now is survey and design work—NOT construction of a wall through the park.” (The statement was also posted near-verbatim on DHS’s X account. ) Unlike in other areas along the border, Scott said, CBP isn’t building a 30-foot wall or installing stadium lighting in Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area. On August 17th, Scott announced that CBP is pausing all construction in Big Bend National Park while he conducts a “personal, on-the-ground evaluation.” Reporters with Marfa Public Radio who flew over the park this morning saw staged construction vehicles, but noted that the crews weren’t working, according to station manager Travis Bubenik. chineseContent: 亚利桑那州前矿业小镇巴塔哥尼亚以南约 22 英里处，沿着一条蜿蜒、未铺砌的山路，路过在开阔牧场上吃草的奶牛，那里矗立着一棵据信至少有 200 年树龄的三叶杨树。这棵被当地人称为“祖母”的树正处于危险之中，并且已经显示出受到压力的迹象，几乎就好像它知道自己的命运一样。叶子过早变黄，在盛夏时掉落在地上。 7 月 27 日，建筑工人砍倒了附近的三棵树，以修建唐纳德·特朗普总统沿美墨边境墙的延伸部分。两天后，一名活动人士爬上了最后一棵树，从那以后，有人坐在悬挂在树枝上的平台上。他们说只要有时间他们就会坐在那里，因为只要有人在树上，它就无法被砍倒。此次抗议活动涉及的不仅仅是一棵三叶杨。 “这棵树实际上代表了反对边境军事化的一条沙线，”生物多样性中心西南地区保护倡导者拉斯·麦克斯帕登说。最近几周，国土安全部重新启动了边境墙建设工作，派出施工人员前往德克萨斯州、亚利桑那州的偏远地区以及托霍诺·奥德姆民族保留地，以完成特朗普的隔离墙，并放弃了环境法来修建隔离墙，引起了从沙漠小镇阿霍到更小的鬼城特林瓜的强烈反对。尽管西南边境的遭遇战数量创历史新低，但最新的建设仍在进行中。事实上，特朗普上任后，西南边境的遭遇几乎立即减少——不是因为任何新的基础设施，而是因为他实际上关闭了庇护。尽管移民过境量急剧下降，但“一大湾”
